ResponsesInList.Title: Tip for linking to Moodle community sites and documentation
ResponsesInList.Text: Hello everyone. Just a tip for those who aren't aware of this, and a friendly reminder for those who are : The Moodle.org forums have some special filters to make it easier to link to community sites, documentation and the tracker. You can see the whole list in the documentation Filters used on the Moodle.org forums but here's a quick summary of some of the things they help you with: Certain Moodle community sites are automatically linked when you simply type their name. So for example, I just need to type Moodle Academy or type MoodleNet or Moodle jobs and the links are automatically made for me.  See more auto-linking phrases in the documentation link I provided above. Tracker issues are automatically linked when you simply type the number. For example I just need to type MDL-79863 and it will automatically link for me. Documentation links can be easily made by adding double square brackets [ [ around the name of the page. We try to have user-friendly pages so for example I type Quiz FAQ and I know it will take me to the Quiz FAQ😉 I can type Upload users and it will link to the docs page about uploading users.  No need to add any underscores between words, and don't add a space between the two brackets. The big advantage of linking to documentation this way is that you will always get linked to the most up to date version of the docs. If you simply paste from Google or even go directly to the docs and copy/paste a page from there, you will be sharing a version-specific link which might get outdated at some point. I hope this helps and I hope it will encourage the community to post more useful links

ResponsesInList.Title: New meeting format Moodle Community Meetings
ResponsesInList.Text: Dear Community, We would like to introduce you to a new meeting format for discussing the many exciting ways Moodle can be used - Moodle Community Meetings. The Moodle Community Meetings are a meeting format from the community for the community and will happen monthly in this Big Blue Button meeting room in the Moodle in English course on moodle.org. The meetings will be rotationally moderated by a group of enthusiastic users who also take care of organizing the meetings. We will kick off the new format on Tuesday 23 September 2025, 1-2 p.m. UTC with a Most of the Moot by the organizers of the Moodle Moot DACH 2025 in Lübeck, Germany. They will give us an introduction to their conference and its unique format of DevCamp and BarCamp and give an overview of the most important discussions and developments that happened there. Generally, the Moodle Community Meetings will cover the challenges and best practices and showcase successful ways of organizing collaboration within Moodle communities. We want to bring together people using Moodle for teaching and learning in all kinds of ways. We will share their questions and knowledge with others to improve Moodle as an open source product and advance open education. The meetings will be held in English but we offer to help other groups interested in community work to initiate meetings in other languages as well. We hope to see you next Tuesday for our first meeting! Feel free to share this announcement on appropriate channels. Kind regards Harald Schnurbusch (RWTH Aachen University, Germany) Marcus Green (Catalyst EU) Don Hinkelman (Moodle Association of Japan) Thomas Niedermaier (University of Münster, Germany) Paul Raper (Switzerland)

ResponsesInList.Title: First Moodle Community Meeting Summary - 23 October 2025
ResponsesInList.Text: On October 23rd, 1-2pm UTC, was the First Moodle Community Meeting , held on the topic of " Most of Moodle DACH " (Germany, Switzerland, Austria). Three academics from the Moodle Association of Germany presented on key points of the largest community gathering in the world, in Lubeck, northern Germany. From Japan, Junko Okabe sensei and I attended. About 25 participants joined during this hour, especially from Europe. We learned the MoodleMoot daily greeting of "Moin", meaning "Good Morning" in German. 昨夜、日本時間22時から23時にかけて、初のMoodleコミュニティミーティングが開催されました。テーマは「Moodle DACH地域（ドイツ、スイス、オーストリア）の現状」です。ドイツMoodle協会の3名の研究者が、ドイツ北部リューベックで開催された世界最大規模のコミュニティ集会の要点を発表しました。岡部順子先生と私が参加しました。「おはよう」を意味する日常の挨拶「モイン」を学びました。 El 23 de octubre, de 13:00 a 14:00 UTC, tuvo lugar la primera reunión de la comunidad Moodle, dedicada al tema «Most of Moodle DACH» (Alemania, Suiza y Austria). Tres académicos de la Asociación Moodle de Alemania presentaron los puntos clave de la mayor reunión comunitaria del mundo, celebrada en Lubeck, en el norte de Alemania. Desde Japón, asistimos Junko Okabe sensei y yo. Alrededor de 25 participantes se unieron durante esta hora, especialmente de Europa. Aprendimos el saludo diario de MoodleMoot, «Moin», que significa «Buenos días» en alemán.  (Traducción realizada con la versión gratuita del traductor DeepL.com) 1. Popularity MoodleDach had 294 registered participants, in an all face-to-face event in northern Germany. Their biggest room held 250 people, so it was standing room only. 参加規模：登録参加者294名、ドイツ西部での完全対面イベント。最大収容250名の会場は立ち見状態となった。 Popularidad: MoodleDach contó con 294 participantes registrados en un evento presencial celebrado en el norte de Alemania. La sala más grande tenía capacidad para 250 personas, por lo que solo había sitio para estar de pie. 2.  Cost: Free conference fee, so each participant only had to pay for their own transport and stay. The eight sponsors above covered the low operating costs. Moodle HQ attended, paying their own way. 費用：参加費無料のため、交通費・宿泊費は各自負担。上記8社のスポンサーが低コストを支援。Moodle HQも自己負担で参加。 Coste: La inscripción a la conferencia era gratuita, por lo que cada participante solo tuvo que pagar su propio transporte y alojamiento. Los ocho patrocinadores mencionados anteriormente cubrieron los bajos costes operativos. Moodle HQ asistió corriendo con sus propios gastos. 3.  DevCamp and BarCamp Format: No refereed or selected presentations--all sessions made ad hoc at the conference. Half of the conference was team programming in a DevCamp (like a Hack Fest). of 22 plugins. And 80 short presentations, which were decided on the morning of the BarCamp days of the conference. Apparently, lots of free coffee was available. DevCampとBarCamp形式： 事前選定された発表はなし。カンファレンスの半分はDevCamp（ハックフェスト形式）でのチームプログラミング（22のプラグイン開発）。残りはBarCamp開催日の朝に決定された80のショートプレゼンテーション。無料コーヒーが豊富に提供された模様。 Formato DevCamp y BarCamp: No hubo presentaciones seleccionadas ni revisadas por pares, todas las sesiones se organizaron de manera ad hoc durante la conferencia. La mitad de la conferencia consistió en programación en equipo en un DevCamp (similar a un Hack Fest). Se presentaron 22 complementos y 80 presentaciones breves, que se decidieron la mañana de los días del BarCamp de la conferencia. Al parecer, hubo mucho café gratis disponible. 4. YouTube Shorts: DACHプログラムのショート動画13本をご覧いただけます： You can view 12 short videos of the DACH program here: Aquí puede ver 12 vídeos cortos del programa DACH: https://www.youtube.com/@MoodlemootDACH https://www.youtube.com/@MoodlemootDACH 5. 多言語対応： 非ドイツ語圏からの参加者40名のため、イベントの半分以上がドイツ語、ほぼ半分が英語で行われました。 Multilingual: There were 40 participants from non-German speaking countries. So over half of the event sesssions were done in English, as well as in German. Multilingüe: Hubo 40 participantes de países no germanoparlantes. Por lo tanto, más de la mitad de las sesiones del evento se llevaron a cabo en inglés, además de en alemán. 6.   Eleven AI summaries available online (most in German): AI要約： オンラインで11件の要約を公開（大半はドイツ語） ： Once resúmenes de IA disponibles en línea (la mayoría en alemán): https://lab.dlc.sh/summaraizer/public/ 日本のMoodleMootでは、初日にワークショップの代わりに、プラグインをプログラミングするDevCampと教材を作成するCourseCampを設けると効果的かもしれません。高いエネルギーと成果が期待できます。MoodleMoot DACHは、MAJカンファレンス主催者に対し、その手順や知見を共有する用意があります。 The MoodleMoot Japan and other community-based Moots might benefit from a DevCamp approach to program plugins, and we wondered about a possible "CourseCamp approach" for educators to make courseware on the first day instead of programming code. These approaches resulted in high energy and high output at DACH. MoodleMoot DACH leadership are willing to share their procedures and insights with MAJ conference organizers. El MoodleMoot Japan y otros Moots comunitarios podrían beneficiarse de un enfoque DevCamp para programar complementos, y nos preguntamos si sería posible un «enfoque CourseCamp» para que los educadores crearan material didáctico el primer día en lugar de programar código. Estos enfoques dieron como resultado una gran energía y un alto rendimiento en DACH. Los responsables de MoodleMoot DACH están dispuestos a compartir sus procedimientos y conocimientos con los organizadores de la conferencia MAJ. コミュニティミーティングの参加者25名全員を、静岡で開催される MoodleMoot Japan に招待しました。STEM、医学教育、言語教育、そしてその先にある分野に重点を置いています。マーカス・グリーン氏も当イベントを推薦してくれました。もし誰かが航空券の資金を手配できるなら、彼も参加したいと考えています。 I invited all 25 participants of the Community Meeting to MoodleMoot Japan in Shizuoka, emphasizing STEM, Medical education, Languages and Beyond. Marcus Green highly recommended this Moot as well. Please post upcoming Moots in Spanish and other languages as a reply to this summary report. Invité a los 25 participantes de la Reunión Comunitaria al MoodleMoot Japón en Shizuoka, haciendo hincapié en STEM, educación médica, idiomas y más allá. Marcus Green también recomendó encarecidamente este Moot. Por favor, publiquen los próximos Moots en español y otros idiomas como respuesta a este informe resumido. The Second Moodle Community Meeting is scheduled for Tuesday, October 28th (the fourth Tuesday of the month) at 1-2pm UTC. Emma Richardson and other participants from the North American Rockies will present and discuss the "Best of Mountain Moot". 第2回Moodleコミュニティミーティングは、10月28日（火）午後1時～2時（UTC）に開催予定です。北米ロッキー山脈地域のエマ・リチャードソン氏ら参加者が 「マウンテン・ムート」 のハイライトを発表・議論します。 La segunda reunión de la comunidad Moodle está programada para el martes 28 de octubre (el cuarto martes del mes) de 13:00 a 14:00 UTC. ResponsesInList.Title: Time to re-organize forums?   Also time to consider approval before a posting is made public in Security forum.
ResponsesInList.Text: Unintended consequences tend to creep in with large/international open sourced projects like Moodle. If one goes to the top level of forums, one will see 'General Help' whose brief description says something to the affect, 'if you don't know where to post, post here!'   If you look at the number of postings in 'General Help' it is by far the most used.   Why is that? How many times does an experience 'helper' suggest to the poster a better forum for their posting?   A bunch!  And depending upon the patience of the poster, (we do live in an 'instant gratification world'), such a suggestion is frustrating and have observered the language in the proper forum reflects that at times. To answer that question is simple ... General Help is at the top!   Suggestion ... put General Help at the bottom thus making the poster scroll down ... hopefully, they will see a more appropriate forum! Security Forum ... due to a recent event, strongly suggest, that forum moderators must approve the posting before it goes public.   It would be the only forum that has that requirement.  Forum moderators are only ones who could possibly verify the poster is who they say they are and validate.  There is potential for a site to fall into being 'held hostage'! Found it somewhat a shock that AI was introduced in 4.5 and there was no forum for it .... added after tool was released. ... which leads to the last .... Now that 5.0 has been released, there is/will be in that series some massive changes.   Might be a good to to start a new 'Verison 5.0' forum ... at the top! :| My 2 cents! 'SoS', Ken

ResponsesInList.Title: Time to re-organize forums?   Also time to consider approval before a posting is made public in Security forum.

ResponsesInList.Title: Time to re-organize forums?   Also time to consider approval before a posting is made public in Security forum.
ResponsesInList.Text: Hello Ken. Thanks for your points, which I’ll raise with the team, as we do agree the forums in Moodle in English need reorganising.There are a lot of forums, as you’re well aware! In fact, that’s one of the reasons for keeping General Help at the top. The  forum description says “If you're not sure where to post, use this forum!”  We actually encourage newbie Moodlers to post there if they’re a bit shy and don’t know their way around our long list of specialised forums. We can always move their post if it’s better placed elsewhere. That’s friendlier than someone taking their first steps here and being told ‘Hey - you should have posted in the [insertname] forum!’ So it would be a big help if you and other dedicated Moodlers could click that ‘report to moderator’ button when you see a post that you think would fit better in a different forum. (That also avoids the poster making a duplicate post before one of us gets a chance to move the original post). You make a good point about a need for forum posts to be moderated before they appear. It’s a shame the functionality doesn’t exist, because I can imagine many organisations finding it really useful. Glad you appreciate the AI forum - we’re reluctant to add new forums because there are so many as it is, but that one does seem to be popular. And although we don’t add forums for specific new versions, your suggestion has given me the perfect opportunity to promote our Moodle Academy What’s new in Moodle 5.0 course (plus webinar) which does indeed include a version-specific forum! 😉

ResponsesInList.Title: Suggestion: Combine "Latest release", "Other supported releases" and "Security-only-supported releases" in to one page
ResponsesInList.Text: To the site administrator Currently there are separate web pages for: Latest release https://download.moodle.org/releases/latest/ Other supported releases https://download.moodle.org/releases/supported/ Security-only-supported releases https://download.moodle.org/releases/security/ Can you combine them all in to one page? That is what many other projects do. For example, PHP downloads https://www.php.net/downloads The argument is, currently the visitor is "automatically" taken to the /latest/, i.e. release 4.2. Many think that it is the *only* supported version and (try to) install of upgrade to it - whether they need it or not - and fail: Some don't have the higher system software needs 4.2 has. Some notorious one-click installers break trying to upgrade. Others are continuously changing a "running horse". The nagging, and too simply formulated, "There is a newer version available" message makes the things worse. The Installing and upgrading help forum is full of examples. In addition, people don't realize that there is a LTS path. On that topic, could you always say 3.9 LTS, 4.1 LTS, when you refer to those releases? I would go a step further and add the development release and the legacy releases on to the same page, see https://www.debian.org/releases/ for example. But this is much less important.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Suggestion: Combine "Latest release", "Other supported releases" and "Security-only-supported releases" in to one page
ResponsesInList.Text: I just want to remind that some years ago, it was done like that (all versions on one page). And i also would prefer to have them all on one page (again). I think it's simpler, avoids one click (and risk of missing information), and let people know what exists (in one page). Perhaps i begin to be an old man (with old habits, and old UI habits), but i prefer a long page (easy to print, search in...) than several little pages with nearly nothing inside, but impliying several clicks. Séverin

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Suggestion: Combine "Latest release", "Other supported releases" and "Security-only-supported releases" in to one page

We'll certainly review and consider the points you've raised with our team. Your feedback is invaluable in helping us improve. Thanks again, Aurélie Community Engagement Lead

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Suggestion: Combine "Latest release", "Other supported releases" and "Security-only-supported releases" in to one page
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Aurélie, Thanks for you answer. My opinion is that there should be pages to download : each of the supported Moodle version (latest, other, security) each of the legacy / unsupported Moodle version development version For the moment, i don't understand why we have : only one version per page, but very big header and footer taking much more place than the real content direct access to the development version from the download home page, but not for supported versions. I suppose there are much more administrators needing supported version than developpers (and these power users should more know how to find development versions, perhaps by git ) Appart from new Moodle installation, or upgrade of Moodle with nearly no plugins (or only very well supported plugins), users should not always take the latest Moodle, but the latest which correctly supports used plugins . And directing them by default to the latest one isn't the best choice. Combining the 3 supported versions, now that 3.9, 3.11 and 4.0 are out of support would not take so much place. I would also like to write again that we had all versions available on the same page for (at least) 10 years, i don't think it was so bad... Best wishes, Séverin

ResponsesInList.Title: Moodle Groups for Crosslisted Course
ResponsesInList.Text:
The enroll table in moodle creates a reference meta link to the child sections , in order to support crosslisted Course. They make use of the enroll plugin to create a meta link to the child section in moodle enrol table, https://moodledev.io/docs/apis/subsystems/enrol#enrol_plugin-add_default_instance . For creating groups under crosslisted group we move the groups of child section to parent Crosslist , but the
challenge is when we uncrosslist a single child section, the enrollment
& groups remain under the crosslisted course and doesn't move back
to the child course. Any other approach we can take on this issue ? This is what the Group api's support https://moodledev.io/docs/apis/subsystems/group

ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Michael, I think the Boost design is clear and structured. Yes, with the switch to Moodle 4.0 the design has been drastically changed in appearance. I'm looking for a switch that will allow me to compress the screen display. In my courses you have to scroll a lot more than before with the new look and feel. But a course looks really better on mobile devices. Numerous design additions for Boost in Moodle 4.0 are implemented in the "Boost Union" theme, such as the display width of courses and the start page. Or favicons. Or the local storage of additional fonts. Or static documents, footnotes, info banners and the "up" button. I particularly like the scroll spy, which ensures that when I switch editing modes, I always end up in the same place in the course I was before. You write that asking if a Moodle site looks good on a mobile device is a mistake. No, I don't think it's a mistake! A very important aspect is the accessibility of the courses and the materials. In many cases, the digital materials are created with analog thinking, namely to print them. A PDF document usually does not have an optimal user experience on a smartphone ... you not only scroll the text up when reading, but also have to constantly slide it to the right and left to be able to read the whole line. I think it is imperative that digital materials and digital platforms adapt to digital devices. Moodle HQ may provide us with statistics that will inform us about the distribution of operating systems and screen sizes when using Moodle worldwide. Diese Statistik würde vielleicht zeigen, dass sehr viel Lernen mit kleinen mobilen Geräten stattfindet und nicht mit großen 24" oder 27" Desktop-PCs. Incidentally, a very special highlight of the new community site is that all content on the start page can be translated using a special tool. So there is now not only the English original, but also versions in French (fr), German (de), Spanish (mx_es) and Japanese (ja). Great! Best regards Ralf Ralf Krause moodleSCHULE e.V.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: The moodle.org new design is now live! - We would like to have your feedback
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Ralf, "You write that asking if a Moodle site looks good on a mobile device is a mistake." No, I did not and I would prefer if something is unclear that you ask before making accusations like that. I wrote that is feels like a mobile first approach which is very normal in todays world. My websites themselves have a responsive design with ~90% mobile users however they also have a design for 4k screens. I'm all for mobile users to have a great experience, I mean I want that myself, but if someone is on a mobile device it can and should be a different theme as it's a different device . If you check your Moodle install under: /moodle/theme/index.php you can choose to have a theme for "Mobile" and "Tablet". Furthermore I recommend all my users to go with the iOS/iPadOS/MacOS (in case of M1) or Android App, especially as you can download everything to view offline. The "Default" theme however should be optimized for desktop and take advantage of the desktop size. It can be responsive but should not be mobile first. I have also looked at "Boost Union" but have not tried it yet. Might do that next week but then again 4.1 should release "soon" so I'll probably just wait until 4.1 is out and the "Boost Union" has been updated for 4.1. "A very important aspect is the accessibility of the courses and the materials." I 100% agree! I think everyone that has made just one course feels that way and wants their course to be as effective as possible. The device the user is on should not matter. "A PDF document usually does not have an optimal user experience on a smartphone" Indeed that is why a course should have all necessary parts within the course. A PDF should only be used as an addition not as a sole source of information. At the end of the day however you will not be as accessible as a desktop and I hope that every mobile user understands this fact. A bigger screen with more resolution just helps. Another option instead of PDF is something like epub most mobile devices have apps that support that and it looks very good on them. "I think it is imperative that digital materials and digital platforms adapt to digital devices." I think this has already happened a few years ago. On a mobile device users should use apps as that is what they are designed for. Especially on iOS, iPadOS or MacOS developers have to adhere to very strict design decisions if they want to be on the App Store. Kind Regards, Michael

ResponsesInList.Title: Announcing the Moodle LMS Community Product Advisory Group
ResponsesInList.Text: Over the last 18 months MoodleHQ has been working to establish a stronger connection with our community in an effort to provide you with more visibility on the work being completed by our teams and to help ensure our priorities are more in line with your needs. Part of this work has included the publication of our public roadmap which provides increased visibility on our plans for the future and the issue of our ‘ Showcase Short ’ news articles, which come out on a regular basis and provide an overview of work being completed by the Moodle HQ Product team. To further support these efforts, today we are delighted to announce the establishment of a new Product Advisory Group (PAG) for Moodle LMS - Community . This group will join our existing PAG groups, the Moodle Workplace PAG (for Moodle Premium Certified Partners) and the Moodle LMS - Partners PAG (for all Moodle Certified Partners) and will be the first one focused on inviting members of our broader community as participants. Just like the Partners and Workplace PAGs, we expect that our newest PAG will be incredibly valuable; allowing a wide variety of voices to be heard efficiently and providing input to our roadmap. The Moodle LMS -  Community PAG will be open to all interested parties, and will be focused on several key activities : Providing a forward view of the existing Moodle LMS Roadmap. Facilitating the ideation of new initiatives and functionality with direct input from the community to influence the roadmap moving forward. Gathering early feedback from the community on the design of features under development. MoodleHQ has been working closely with the Moodle Users Association on the creation of this PAG. Its formation is an initiative which is being completed in partnership with the association and in parallel to the recent change announcement issued by the MUA . By establishing the Moodle LMS - Community PAG, all interested MUA members will have an alternative avenue to shape the future of Moodle LMS. As part of the next evolution of the MUA, we hope that it will prove to be as successful as its predecessor, helping to drive many more great initiatives and continue to drive alignment between the community and MoodleHQ into the future. Over the coming days we will be posting more details about the Moodle LMS - Community PAG , its operation, and meeting schedules.  The first of which will be a kick off meeting to disucss further the intent and operation of the Moodle LMS - Community PAG.  Additionally a dedicated Community PAG space will be established on Moodle.org.   I would like to invite any parties who wish to participate to please indicate their interest by responding to the announcement thread here . EDIT: Please note the link to the MUA announcement has been updated as they have now provided a public link.

ResponsesInList.Text: The PAG will be based more around gathering feedback and insight from the community in a structured way through early involvement with the prioritisation and design process. It will vary on how that feedback is gathered and incorporated into the work plan. Unlike the MUA where "projects" were voted on, i.e. a defined piece of funtionality was put up for voting to be funded, which was problematic on a number of fronts, this will be more about shaping a piece of work collectively to get to the best outcome for all. My hope that this group will not just be reviewing work being undertaken by HQ but be a means that other groups doing significant work can seek structured feedback as well, but once the PAG is up that might be something we can look to tackle if there is interest as the PAG ramps up. Regarding the existing MUA memebers, the membership to the PAG will be open to MUA members first in recognition of the contribution that the MUA has made over many years, then the rest of the community. ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Announcing the Moodle LMS Community Product Advisory Group
ResponsesInList.Text: Thanks for the question. There were a number of fronts where this process was inhibiting the Moodle community to deliver the best possible product.  From discussions with the MUA committee these feelings were also shared by a significant number of the MUA members as well.  I only point this out to reinforce that the move to a PAG was a mutual decision between HQ and the MUA itself and not something imposed by HQ by any measure. Representation - At its core the MUA had a representation model that favored members who made larger financial contributions. This as a consequence tended to favor projects coming from the larger institutions, 13 institutions (3.5% of the membership) held 42% of the available votes. As a result, at times development resources were being directed to areas of the system that, while needing improvement, may not be areas which were providing the highest impact across the system for the whole user base.  This is always a challenge for any product at the best of times.  The PAG will be separating financial contributions from the feedback and input that we will be seeking from the community to ensure the most representative input we can from the PAG. This will apply to all contributions to the overall roadmap as well as individual pieces of development. HQ Split priorities and resourcing - Frequently Projects being proposed by the MUA were not related to areas of work that HQ was currently engaging in improving.  This led to teams in HQ working on the MUA project + internal projects in 2 different parts of the system.  This constant context switching causes a level of inefficiency for the teams and lost productivity and a lower ability for HQ to deliver.  In addition the size of projects was inherently limited by the voting cycle, largely anything larger than 1 release was very difficult to tackle as there was an expectation for a new project each voting cycle.  This frequently leads to either incomplete implementations or some projects just never being considered. The move to the PAG will address this by tackling improvements and projects which parallel planned improvements allowing greater overall efficiency, and greater potential scope. Product Focus - Probably the largest down side of the MUA voting process was the output was an already defined pieces of work that defined a piece of functionality prior to voting.  In many ways this is counter to a good product process which seeks to understand the problem space, looks at a wide variety of solutions and seeks to refine the best one.  The vast majority of proposals propose a technical solution without a clear problem definition or put another way is focusing on the solution rather than developing an understanding of what it's trying to solve. Product Management Approach -The introduction of the PAG will allow us to apply a holistic product management methodology to identifying, ideating and solutioning on issues that matter to our community, something we couldn't always do in an MUA context. We will start with identifying the core issues through prioritisation processes, using synchronous and async tasks ideate and brainstorm potential solutions, narrowing down to a preferred solution, and ultimately defining the required functionality.  I'm in the process of scheduling the PAG kickoff meeting (announcement soon) during which we will discuss this approach using relevant examples to make it come to life. I hope this helps the understanding of the direction that the PAG is headed and how we hope the MUA members continue to contribute to the direction of the product.

ResponsesInList.Title: Langauage customisation error
ResponsesInList.Text: While trying to do language customisation  for moodle 4..12 , facing this error . Any suggestion

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Langauage customisation error
ResponsesInList.Text: When I've hit this problem in the past, it is usually because of a language string somewhere on the site that used capital letters in the identifier. From memory, the problem is that when the language string uses capital letters in the code, it ends up being written all lower-case into the custom language files, then it doesn't recognise them as the same. When it tries to write both into the database , it then hits a duplicate issue, as the database recognises them as being the same language string and has an index in place that prevents duplicates (which then causes the error). The solution, as far as I can remember, is to first turn on Debugging for your site, to get a better error message, then look for the language string identifier it complains about in the code. If you fix that language string identifier to be all lower case in the code (if it hasn't already been fixed to lower case), then check to see if it is all lower case in the custom files, then manually empty the custom language string database table (sorry, I can't remember the table name off the top of my head), purge caches and try again. (As an aside, this question doesn't relate to any of the Moodle community sites hosted at moodle.org, so should probably be moved to a more appropriate forum).

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Pb lors de la mise à jour de Moddle
ResponsesInList.Text:
These environment checks are listed in 
```text
admin/environment.
xml
```
 and the functions for each checks are in `lib/upgradelib.php` . You have Moodle 3.11.5 but the check which is failing, check_xmlrpc_usage, was only added in Moodle 3.11.9 (as part of MDL-71747 ). So this check should not exist in your Moodle version. Is it possible you have the wrong `admin/environment.xml` ? One that is newer than your Moodle version? Maybe first upgrading to the latest Moodle 3.11.x (currently 3.11.12) will resolve the error.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: PHP 8 version issue with single sign on with Moodle-Mahara
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Nitin, Moodle 4.1.x doesn't need the XML -RPC extension anymore, that requirement was removed @ MDL-70889 . And, more specifically, all the MNet functionality now is performed by a PHP library instead of the PHP extension. See MDL-76055 for more information. So far, the functionality (SSO / roaming) was tested in that issue and, also, in the QA cycle that happened before the Moodle 4.1 release. In any case, bugs happen, so I would recommend you to gather all the possible information (versions both sides, configuration details without any secret sharing, exact steps... debugging information...) and then create an issue in the Tracker to see if we can reproduce the problem. With good reproduction steps, surely the fix will be easier to implement. Ciao

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Why are the links so "bold" on the moodle.org forums?
ResponsesInList.Text: Accessibility is about helping as many people as possible with a focus on helping those with disabilities. Ramps help those pushing prams, cyclists and those in wheelchairs. Similarly, underlining links helps many people who are colour blind to tell when particular text is a link, but it can also help those viewing a webpage in a bright setting (outside or in a bright teaching space). You can read more about the wider benefits of accessibility and the social model of disability in the Moodle Academy Introduction to Accessibility course . Please can everyone also abide by the Moodle.org code of conduct and avoid making comments personal. Constructive feedback is welcome, but please discuss the issue rather than making the comments personal attacks on others. We want moodle.org forums to be a welcoming place for everybody in our community to share their ideas and suggestions. Thank you.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Moodle Docs MediaWiki upgrade checklist
ResponsesInList.Text: As promised, here's a checklist: Edit Mediawiki:Sidebar to create a top menu on non-front pages e.g. https://docs.moodle.org/311/en/index.php?title=MediaWiki%3ASidebar&type=revision&diff=140895&oldid=108183 Edit any page with blocks and replace it with a Bootstrap 4 card deck e.g. https://docs.moodle.org/311/en/index.php?title=Main_page&type=revision&diff=140780&oldid=140215 Search and replace `class="nicetable"` with `class="wikitable"` Search and replace code tags with syntaxhighlight e.g. https://docs.moodle.org/311/en/index.php?title=ad-hoc_contributed_reports&curid=11193&diff=140868&oldid=140381 Edit MediaWiki:Helplogin-url and add a link to the login help page in the wiki e.g. https://docs.moodle.org/311/en/index.php?title=MediaWiki:Helplogin-url&oldid=140855 I've done 1. for most wikis, though feel free to make changes. Thanks again to everyone for helping and let me know if you'd like me to help with anything.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Moodle Docs MediaWiki upgrade
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Helen! I am currently writing the documentation for my recently approved "Random select answers question type" plugin. In the new MediaWiki version, for the 3rd-party question types, there seems to be a conflict between 2 blocks which should both appear in the column on the right. They are the {{Questions}} block and the {{Infobox plugin...} block. In almost all of the existing 3rd-party question types doc, the doc page first displays the long list of core question types, followed by the relevant documentation for the current question type, which I find rather confusing for the visitor. If one places the {{Questions}} block before the {{Infobox plugin...} block, it goes to the column on the right, and the {{Infobox plugin...} block remains in the main column, at the top, which IMHO looks better. Actually, I feel one could to without the {{Questions}} block altogether, since users arriving on a particular 3rd-party question type page are first of all interested in its documentation, not in links to core question types. What do you think?

ResponsesInList.Title: Are there too many Moodle in English forums?
ResponsesInList.Text: Something Ive been thinking about for a while. I tend to hang out in the themes forum, but occasionally will pop into Lesson and try to answer a few questions there. I don't really have the bandwidth for much more than that, not so much because the forums arent that busy, but because hopping in and out of forums is a bit tedious and my inbox couldnt handle being subscribed to more. So, I was thinking, would it be a good idea to merge many of the forums together.  My thoughts would be something like: Installing / Server / Admin Support General Help Teaching and Learning ( including course design ) Activities ( all of them, and I feel a lot of these would fall under the concept of teaching and learning) Plugins Themes and UX Development Obviously, a lot of this is dependent on individual forum traffic, but many of the forums are quite slow and I believe would benefit from being merged together to focus more eyes on the requests and suggestions therein. Thoughts?

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Are there too many Moodle in English forums?
ResponsesInList.Text: I do agree there are many forums, and I feel some cleanup could help, but having separate forums allows for better control over who Moderates which, and allows for better control over what's coming into my inbox. I read the daily digests every morning and it's huge, but because there are many forums I have turned off entirely (because they'll just never apply to me, such as Installing, Server , Development), I am able to keep my digest relevant to my interests. However, I'd not want to lose access to things if combined, such as Admin Support, since I am a Moodle Administrator (i'm just on a Hosted environment). If there's a particular thread in a forum that's getting large and it doesn't apply to me (which tends to happen in the General forum), I launch it from my daily digest and then I unsubscribe to that particular thread (but I'd like to do that as needed, and not constantly if forums were combined). I actually wish there were more forums for the "Plugins" -- one for every single activity plugin and block plugin. (For example, I feel the Completion Progress Block thread is so long and unwieldy that I can never go back and find what I need -- it would benefit from having threads instead of being one long forum post that dates back years...)

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Training Task Question: Read the input parameter value
ResponsesInList.Text: Well, I can see a few things in there that you might want to think about: You have defined a form, but you've not added a 'submit' button to it (I'm assuming this is covered in the course, but $this->add_action_buttons() is probably what you're looking for). You've used 'required_param()' on the page, which means there will be an error when it is viewed before the form has been submitted, so you may well want to replace this with a call to 'optional_param()' instead (as that will cope if the param is missing) - as an aside, you might want to pick a better variable name than $courseid, maybe $name? Your defined form is not actually instantiated or output - somewhere in the code (outside the 'simplehtml_form' class definition), you need to add a couple of lines: $form = new simplehtml_form(); $form->display(); After that, there's still quite a bit of tidy-up to do, but hopefully those 3 changes will get the basics working.

ResponsesInList.Title: User documentation improvements
ResponsesInList.Text: Following the UX Survey results in which help documentation was highlighted as an area needing improvement, Mary and I talked with Moodle Senior UX designer, Hina, about what we could learn from the survey comments and where to start on making user documentation improvements. We came up with a number of action points as follows: Improve each of the activity start pages, such as Assignment activity , to provide a quick guide for the activity, with more detailed information about settings etc. added to other activity pages. Make it clearer whether documentation applies to teachers or to admins by using the heading 'Site administration settings' on activity settings pages. Investigate adding a note at the top of pages with info for admins only. Go through all activity pages, checking the 'See also' links are up to date and making consistency improvements. Go through tracker issues labelled docs_required and add user documentation where necessary according to the Docs required issues process . Delete pages in the 3.9 docs for plugins not updated for 3.5 (see pages linking to the infobox plugin template for the list of plugin documentation pages). Identify areas of the documentation which need rewriting and reorganising to make the information easier to understand. You may have noticed that Mary and I are already working on some of these action points. As always, if you can help in any way with the documentation it would be much appreciated! Many thanks to all our documentation contributors, including everyone helping with documentation in other languages.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: User documentation improvements
ResponsesInList.Text: help documentation was highlighted as an area needing improvement,.. What an understatement! If you mean the https://docs.moodle.org/XY/ wikis, they are broken beyond mere improvement. Only a complete rewrite/redesign could bring something useful - time spent on "improvements" is lost time.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: User documentation improvements
ResponsesInList.Text: I disagree.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: User documentation improvements
ResponsesInList.Text: Well, I didn't expect much agreement, there were no arguments to agree. Wasn't inclined to spend time, because that time too will be wasted. Still put that note, because I saw that valuable resources are diverted to this fruitless task. Now you've asked and may be others are raising eye brows, here's an ultra short version. I will not discuss or explain this any further. If there is sufficient demand, I will sit down and collect the forum threads going back to at least a decade. The biggest reason for failure is that the MoodleDocs is completely organic. No ToC, no chapters/volumes (think of the sub-systems that were added to Moodle the last couple of years), no quality checking. People create loose pages on impulse then leave. And the official maintainers make a stand saying they are non-technical and do only administrative work. Ironically the biggest administrative work, duplicating the wikis every six months, makes matters worse exponentially. Outdated information are just being moved forward. Every time somebody comes up with a problem, the standard answer is, "It is a wiki. Please update yourself!" The person could be anybody, who just ventured without a clue. There are other problems. No point in discussing them as long as the mentality above remains.

ResponsesInList.Title: Moodle.org needs a better forum software
ResponsesInList.Text: I realize that this might be somewhat contentious, but I think Moodle.org desperately needs a better forum software, to organize and facilitate the increasing amount of discussion that this community creates. It's easy to google moodle.org, but otherwise very hard to stay on top of all the relevant discussions. Moodle's forum activity is great for course use, but not optimal for this kind of use. Discourse (discourse.org) would be a much, much, better alternative. I'll be happy to extrapolate my argument if there is any chance of this being considered.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Moodle.org needs a better forum software
ResponsesInList.Text: The Moodle.org forum software is the forum software for Moodle itself. This means that it incorporates features and integrations specifically aimed at education. By using it for Moodle.org it means it is heavily tested by the organisation developing it, and it is free/libre software.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Moodle.org needs a better forum software
ResponsesInList.Text: I did not suggest the forum to be replaced by a closed-source software, on the contrary, the potential candidate for replacement I mentioned is open source. Also, I would dispute the fact that moodle.org forums are needed for the purposes of a test installation. My suggestion rose from the opinion that with a modern forum software, moodle.org would be even better a place to learn, discuss and share things about Moodle than it already is. Even if Moodle.org keeps using Moodle's forums, I suggest you look at Discourse, it's a great piece of software. =)

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Moodle.org needs a better forum software
ResponsesInList.Text: It might be worth highlighting MoodleNet at this point too, for discussions around Moodle.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Moodle.org needs a better forum software
ResponsesInList.Text: Yeah, I'm really excited about MoodleNet , but isn't that mostly about learning resources and not the "meta" (Moodle as software)?

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Moodle.org needs a better forum software
ResponsesInList.Text: I think it goes deeper than that: 'Here is this wonderful piece of education software, built with forums for your students to communicate in class' 'Here is this magnificent community that uses forums to discuss said wonderful piece of software' ' Ah, so I'll be able to see the forums from this tool actually in use' ' Oh no, we don't think they're good enough for us to use - but you should really use them with your students!' Yep, I can see that going down well in presentations to HE/FE/3rd sector decision-makers, all across the world. Now, that isn't saying Moodle's forums can't/shouldn't be improved (they certainly can be, and are being) - but we should ( IMO ) be using as much of Moodle as we can for relevant purposes (such as forums) and if that leads to improvements being made through pointing out alternative/better ways of doing things, then so much the better (there's already the MoodleOverflow discussion forum type in the plugins database , which I think is excellent, personally)

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Moodle.org needs a better forum software

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Moodle.org needs a better forum software
ResponsesInList.Text: P.S. What's wrong with the Moodle forum? What features does it lack? Why do those features benefit an educational focus? Where's the funding coming from to implement those changes?

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Moodle.org needs a better forum software
ResponsesInList.Text: Ok I didn't realize my little post would get such a hearty response. I have a very specific use case in mind that I'll explain, though I'm certain it's out of scope. I am using Moodle to set up an internal training program within a research institution. Videos of in-person workshops and recordings of webinars, among other content, will be turned into on demand trainings. We already use Discourse as a communications platform. If each of the courses had a forum that was hosted on the same Discourse instance, then it would allow these two platforms to compliment each other. The forum activity could have an extended life outside of the moodle course. > How do those features benefit an educational focus? Our educational focus is specifically one that is demand driven. We'll post content as it becomes available. And if there is a demand for a particular training, we can respond to it. A stand-alone forum that is also integrated into an LMS could help keep the flow of information more open and flexible, making the community more responsive to training needs.

Any suggestions on good practices to write documentation ? Thanks in advance ;-* Zabelle

ResponsesInList.Title: Docs
ResponsesInList.Text: Hello Zabelle. The English language documentation has different wikis for each version, identified by the number in the URL so if you have written your documentation in the 3.5 version then (assuming the plugin is also current for the 3.6 and 3.7 versions) then you would have to rewrite the page separately for those two versions - or we can do it for you if you prefer. When a new version of Moodle comes out the documentation is redirected to the lastest version, so now if you simply type docs.moodle.org/en/Teamup, (with no version number) you will be taken to the latest version which is 3.7. The good news is that, if you add your page to the 3.7 documentation it will be copied over to future versions so you won't need to do it again.) The French language documentation is slightly different because they just have one version, as you have discovered, 3x, for all 3.+ versions of Moodle.

ResponsesInList.Title: Moodle documentation: Where is the software architecture documentation?
ResponsesInList.Text: I write this after spending hours searching the web and the moodle sites looking for clues about the architecture of Moodle. As a software architect tasked with the job of evaluating the architecture of Moodle I find that I'm faced with the task of actually documenting the various aspects (views) of the architecture before I can evaluate it. Perhaps it would be helpful for me to describe what it is I want to see. The three main questions I'm trying to answer are: What are the major elements that make up the architecture? What are the roles and responsibilities of the elements? What are the relationships between the elements? I want to see some documentation that describes the code structures and their relationships (module views), the runtime structures and their relationships (component and connector views), and documentation that describes how the structures interact with non-software elements such as humans and hardware (allocation views). There are multiple ways to document all of these views. Not all are required, but here are some examples. Examples of module views: Decomposition view (focuses on is-part-of relationships) Uses view (focuses on depends-on relationships) Generalization view (focuses on is-a relationships) Layered view (focuses on the layering of the system, each layer could be thought of as a virtual machine) Examples of component and connector views:

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Moodle documentation: Where is the software architecture documentation?
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi, Steve, Welcome to Moodle. I think that the folks over at the General Developer Forum can either answer many of your questions or point you in the right direction. If you do not in a day or two get the responses you need here, you might want to post over there. You can imagine how busy the developers are, but they really do try to be as helpful as possible. Good luck in your quest! Regards, Art

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Moodle documentation: Where is the software architecture documentation?
ResponsesInList.Text: You are asking the wrong question. It is like you are asking for engineering plans of someone's back yard, or of a city park. They don't exist, and they don't exist because they would not be much use. Moodle is not rocket science. It is a bunch of fairly simple and common stuff, like web forums, wikis, etc. What makes it really good is that all this stuff is packaged together in a way that is really easy to use for teaching. So Moodle is like a city park that has only ordinary trees and grass and walkways, but which is a really nice relaxing place to sit and eat your lunch, or go for a jog. That is, without any high tech, it fulfils its function really well. And Moodle is a city park where the authorities invite the local people in to help tend the plants and rake the gravel. Most of these people are coming in on their own time, in the evening or weekends, and most of them aren't specialists. They would not understand engineering plans, even if they existed, and they would certainly not want to contribute if they had to spend lots of time updating plans as well as gardening. They just want to sit around and chat for a bit (Moodle forums) so they can reach a consensus about how their park should be, then they just want to get on and make it happen. Anyway, it is fairly plain to see how it all works just by looking at the park itself. Similarly, if you want to see how any particular part of Moodle works, just look at the code itself. For posting this forum reply, I am using mod/forum/post.php. My brower is telling me where the code for that is. That file will call a whole lot of library functions, but while looking at the code in my editor, I just hold down CTRL and click on the function name, and I am taken to where that function is defined. And all the code is pretty transparent. It should be clear what it does, there aren't any intentional pitfalls to trap the unwary. Now, if you are a professional software developer, this culture takes a lot of getting used to, and frequently is very annoying. But the reason that Moodle is such a great educational tool is that it was built by educators, and not by engineers. If you are a professional engineer, you will have serious doubts about the quality of the workmanship; but if you are a teacher or a student, you will like what you see, and be blissfully unaware of all the duct tape and string holding it together underneath. Tim - professional developer, who was forced to work on Moodle against his will, and finally got the lack of archetecture after about 6 months. P.S. In fact, there is a name for the type of archetecture that Moodle uses. If you read Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture you will find that there are names for the simple techniques that Moodle uses. I read it some time ago, so I have forgotten which names they were. I think 'Transaction Script' was one. I must look it up and post it on MoodleDocs , so there is somewhere to direct people who ask this question.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Moodle documentation: Where is the software architecture documentation?
ResponsesInList.Text: Thank you. I appreciate that this is the approach Moodle has taken. I can see that Moodle has been very successful and that many places have adopted it as their LMS. I'm glad it's an free and open source system. However, if a group asked you to explain why Moodle is an architecturally better choice for an LMS than WebCT, Blackboard, Sakai, Angel, Atutor, Desire2Learn, ELGG, Drupal, Joomla, or no LMS at all. What would you say? What would you use to justify your response? Consider that the group's working definition of "software architecture" was: " The software architecture of a program or computing system is the structure or structures of the system, which comprise software elements, the externally visible properties of those elements, and the relationships among them. " (CMU/SEI) Consider also that the group believed the following statement was true. "If all that mattered was functionality, any software architecture would do."

What documentation there is about architecture and coding standards ( http://docs.moodle.org/en/Coding and http://docs.moodle.org/en/Moodle_architecture ) is all about making it as easy as possible for people to set up, use and modify.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Moodle documentation: Where is the software architecture documentation?
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Will, I am not so sure it is arrogance as much as it is perspective. Certainly your comments are familiar. My non-software experience leads me to conclude from a cultural point of view, those two terms are often related. These comments probably belong in the social forum but ... I break the rules sometimes. Speaking for myself, I know nothing about architectural frameworks for software documentation. As a software system integrator and support person for several private companies in a previous life, documentation of code was the #1 complaint around the water cooler of those who improved somebody else's code. These people were talking like new users. All I could do was be emotionally sympathetic. Everybody can do what they can do. I decided that one of the big areas of improvement for a new user was to edit the first paragraph on any page in MoodleDocs. I limit myself to 'teacher documentation' areas and feel there is still lots of work to do. I have not figured out how to motivate more people to assist in this "great work". I generally don't touch developer pages, because I am ignorant and "I don't care about those arrogant types who assume everyone knows the basics and pick nits". Listen to my potentially arrogant perspective: it is not how the imperfect hammer is made that is important, but how you teach somebody to use the it. With humor I now say, "is it any wonder that only the ignorant listen to me?" And yes I have looked at some PHP code. What about those cute, or obviously frustrated, or really cryptic comments placed there by people since the beginning of time? That is not documentation which is really user friendly in any perspective. Moodle has the classic problem of allocation of resources, in an open source environment. Do "You have a" solution for "us"? Best Chris

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Moodle documentation: Where is the software architecture documentation?
ResponsesInList.Text: I missed the original post too, and being incapable of shutting up about stuff like this - a few observations... I think it's often a matter of perspective. The original poster wanted to do an in-depth analysis of Moodle's architecture so that he could compare it with other systems. I'm surprised that nobody asked him why he wanted to do that. It all sounds very worthy but does the result actually have any meaning in the real world? Will, your point or some variation on it comes up very regularly. Firstly, I completely agree. Code is not documentation and examples are not documentation. Projects that (yes, often arrogantly) suggest that is a perfectly reasonable substitute for documentation need a good slap I don't feel that Moodle is one of them. Moodle has been put together over a number of years by a lot of people, some professional developers, some keen amateurs. Some wrote documentation, some didn't. Some kept documentation up to date, some didn't. However, what are we supposed to do - "you can't submit that code until it is fully documented with UML (God help us)" etc etc? ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Moodle documentation: Where is the software architecture documentation?
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Mark, I loved your work flow for assignments - brilliant, and explanatory, very good indeed. The problem for me, just me, is it falls into the Chasm of Serious Unconcern. In short, as one falls into the chasm one thinks only of "who cares?". Obvious you do - sufficiently to take the time out to do it and more power to you and to anyone who looks at it and takes something from it. Personally, I do not have either the time or the inclination to take the time to do anything like that - and I doubt many Moodlers, even serious Moodlers, would. Süreç's diagram is good too, but is it really necessary? Perhaps for some people, but not for others. <rant class="rambling_response"> Will, My personal preference is for two things, the first is that is this idea going to make my lessons and classes better? Second, as my understanding of Moodle grows, can I keep sufficient technobabble out of my responses to questions asked? Arrogant, ybya it is. I love episodes of Star Trek:TNG and Voyager, every episode they do that technobabble extremely well. It is like listening to an economist speak, meaningless nonsense really, but it makes weird sense because it sounds so good. That kind of jargonistic approach to technical subjects has influenced a whole range of documentation, you only have to read a Microsoft help file to see that. Same with Moodle. Chris Collman is fighting it, and has been cleaning up some of my obvious babbledoms, for which I am eternally grateful, even though I am trying to avoid it. If you go back to the original question of this thread, you can see that what is being asked for is documentation that is full of this technobabble. It is this that we need to be arguing against, not being complicit in evolving it, allowing it to grow. All that does is to keep ordinary people out of it. If that is being arrogant, then mea culpa. This line "As a software architect tasked with the job of evaluating the architecture of Moodle..." Why on earth would you want to? Moodle is a tool - a useful tool - but a tool nonetheless. It is an effective content management system, it can be used in a number of contexts. It is online - therefore connectionless - has relative security - not that strong no-one can get into it, but not that poor that anyone can get into it. The answer to that job that Steve has is "Who cares?" Does it work? Can we use it? How much? These are the important questions when evaluating any software. I am sure if Steve was to ask Microsoft for this documentation for Windows 7 I am sure he would get a blank stare, then everyone would be too busy laughing to deliver a coherent response. Evaluating Moodle's architecture is easy because you only need to look at the directory tree to see how it would work. Why clutter all that up with pages and pages of documentation and artwork extolling the virtues of technobabble that achieves little or nothing. ( IMNSHO much of that sort of thing has the bottom line of "Look at this, it proves I am just brilliant so bow your head in the face of genius", actually.) Moodle has the advantage of allowing people to just being able to get involved at so many different levels, from a User of someone else's work all the way up to Developer. It is like Moodle demands from you only what you think you want to give it and this needs be encouraged. My suspicion is that too few people, like me, are interested in finding out what the technobabble really means so they would contribute little or nothing. Easy excuse not to if the first words you run into are words that make spaghetti of a reasonable person's perception of Moodle. For me, it gave me to opportunity to get involved in developing something that I can see is useful that has a future if it is conserved and carefully managed. I make a minuscule contribution in repayment for the hours of simple fun I have being involved, of pleasure learning about Moodle - even just in the forums. I could not contribute in any other way - I have neither the skill or patience. But my paltry efforts are appreciated by a lot of people - even if they never know I who I am or what I have done. I don't care, I am simply having fun, and if that is arrogant, then so mote it be. </rant> New Motto: "Let there be no short answers for such questions!!!!"

ResponsesInList.Text: I have just read this entire thread and my reaction is  - wow - do I really want to get involved in such a closed minded group?  Let me explain...  I am a software engineer recently hired by a school and tasked with examining Student Information Systems and, specifically, Moodle to supplement an existing in-house developed system.  Integration will be required to allow both to work together.  So my first thought was to learn how Moodle works and determine the level of effort.  I found this development forum and this is the first thread with a title resembling my task.  What do I find but a query into how Moodle works that has been responded with little constructive information and a lot of 'we don't do it that way because we don't understand or agree with the need'. I'd like to explain why such documents are important.  First, it is not 'technobabble'.  That term refers to language that has no discreet meaning and whose purpose is to impress/entertain without real underlying substance.  Steve was not looking for meaningless diagrams or wordy description, but rather an accurate description of how Moodle works.  I have the same need.  A description of the architecture would provide the information that I can use to evaluate the system and also enhance it when/if the need arises.  Another result of such information is the ability to make comparisons and evaluate which is the better solution to a problem.  A third benefit is knowing what specific portion relates to the current task.  If you consider this paragraph 'technobabble' then I would respond "I do not think that word means what you think it means". (I nod to "The Princess Bride" for that wonderful quote).  If the docs truly are technobabble then they should either be a) discarded because they have no meaning or b) to be re-written in accurate, understandable language.  Docs that can't be understood are meaningless, but that doesn't mean there should be no documentation, nor should it be dumbed down for general public consumption.  Unfortunately, the computer world invented it's own language, just as the medical, physics, and any other newly developed effort must do to describe that which is new. <rant_on>As an IT professional I find such outright rejection in this forum of what I daily use to perform the task at hand highly offensive.  This is not being elitist or exclusive.  It does mean that I expect to be given a certain amount of respect for the 29 years of experience that I bring to the table. I GUARANTEE that I could be a valuable, contributing member of this community, but I'm not sure I want to confront the attitudes I have found.<rant_off> Proper modification/enhancement of any system requires that the system be understood.  Would you want your doctor to begin surgery without knowing how your body works?  How about your auto mechanic?  Please open your minds to the possibility that there exists the need to have documentation that describes Moodle.  It is not enough to that it works.  Understanding HOW it works is vital for worthwhile results. My current task of understanding Moodle seems very daunting and dark at this moment.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Moodle documentation: Where is the software architecture documentation?
ResponsesInList.Text: If you have specific questions about how Moodle works, please ask them here. One of the more interesting things that has been written about how Moodle works is Pedagogy . Particularly the " Social Constructionism as a Referent" section. Point 4. there is relevant. To explain something to someone, you need to know where they are coming from. What they already know. It is probably futile to expect a single Moodle architecture document to satisfy everyone. On the other hand, that is not an excuse not to try to explain the basic bits that everyone wants to know. What should such a document say. Let's try drafting something: (where it makes a difference - not many places - I describe Moodle 2.0) Overview of a Moodle installation Moodle is a Learning Management System, Course Management System, or Virtual Learning Environment, depending on which term you prefer. It goal is to give teachers and students the tools they need to teach and learn. Although it comes from a background of Social Constructionist pedagogy , it can be used to support any style of teaching and learning. Moodle is a web application written in PHP. Moodle is open source. Copyright is owned by individual contributors, not assigned to a single entity, although the company Moodle Pty Ltd in Perth Australia, owned by Moodle's founder Martin Dougiamas, manages the project. A Moodle installation comprises the Moodle executing in a PHP-capable web server; a database managed by MySQL , PostgreSQL , Microsoft SQL Server, or Oracle ; and a file store for uploaded and generated files (the moodledata folder). All three parts can run on a single server, or they can be separated with many load-balanced web-servers, a database cluster, and a file-server. Or anywhere between those extremes. Moodle as a modular system Like many successful open source systems, the moodle structured as a core system, surrounded by numerous plugins to provide specific functionality. Plugins in Moodle are of specific types. That is, and authentication plugin and an activity module will communicate with Moodle core using very different APIs each specifically tailored to the type of functionality the plugin will provide. Functionality common to all plugins (installation, upgrade, permissions, configuration, ...) are, however, handled consistently across all plugin types. The standard Moodle distribution includes Moodle core and a number of plugins of each type, so that out of the box, Moodle provides a lot of functionality. By installing and removing plugins, a particular Moodle installation can be adapted for a particular purpose. Physically, a Moodle plugin is just a folder of PHP scripts (and CSS , JavaScript , etc. if necessary). Moodle core communicates with the plugin by looking for particular entry points, often defined in the file lib.php within the plugin. Moodle core Moodle core provides the infrastructure necessary to build an LMS by supporting the following concepts. A course, which is a sequence of activities organised into sections . Courses are organised into a hierarchical set of categories within a Moodle site. Users, profile, my moodle ... ( sorry, can't be bothered to explain all this now, will just make notes. ) Groups and Cohorts ... Contexts, roles, capabilities, and permissions, ... Activity and course completion ... Navigation, settings and configuration ... Installation, upgrade ... Logs, reporting, statistics ... The most important plugin types Activities (and resources ) - the individual items that make up a course. The main tools for teaching and learning. For example forum, wiki, quiz, .... Activities are by far the largest type of plugin in terms of amount of code. I forum or wiki system could be a software project in its own right. Blocks - small bits of functionality that can be added to the sides (normally) of other pages. Many blocks provide views of data that is available elsewhere, allowign that information to be displayed on the course page, for example. Themes - The overall visual style of a Moodle site, or of a particular course, or all courses in a category, can be changed by selecting a different theme. Language packs - Moodle is internationalised, and you can get language packs for many languages. http://download.moodle.org/langpack/2.0/ . (Individual user-interface strings can be customised in any Moodle installation from within the admin screens.) Course formats - Controls how the structure of the course, a sequence of activities grouped into sections, is presented to the users. Authentication plugins - Controls how users log in. Moodle can manage usernames and passwords itself, or use those stored in LDAP or another database. Alternatively, Moodle can use a number of single-sign-on schemes. Enrolment plugins - Controls which users are enroled in which courses. Again this can be by synchronising with another system, perhaps a student information system, or it can be tracked internally by Moodle. Repository plugins - Ways for users to get content (files) into Moodle. Either by uploading from their hard drive, or by getting the file from another location on the Internet, perhaps Drop Box, Google Docs, or Flickr. There are many more types of plugins (more than 30 at the last count). These include text filters, question types, gradebook reports, admin reports, course reports, plagiarism detection services and web service protocols. How Moodle code is organised Moodle follows mostly a transaction script approach. That is, suppose you are looking a a Forum. The URL will be .../mod/forum/view.php, and that is the PHP script that will be in overall control of the display of that page. However, behind that basic transaction script approach, a lot of the core functionality has be refactored out into libraries (mostly in the .../lib folder). This provides something of a domain model. (However, the Moodle project started before PHP was capable of supporting object-oriented code, so don't expect an object-oriented domain model.) HTML is mainly output through renderer classes. These allow different plugins to generate a consistent user-interface, which the themes can control. So, for example, there is an $OUTPUT->box($contents); method. The Moodle database The Moodle database has a database that comprises many tables (more than 250) because the whole database is an aggregate of the core tables and the tables belonging to each plugin. However, this large database can be understood because the tables for one particular plugin typically only link to each other, and a few core tables. The Moodle database structure is defined in install. xml files (inside the DB folder in each plugin, and lib/db for Moodle core). To see those definitions in human-readable form, you can go to Admin -> Development -> XMLDB editor, and click on the [Doc] link. -------------- OK, how is that for a first draft. It is longer than I was hoping, What could be missed out? Also, what is missing.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Moodle documentation: Where is the software architecture documentation?
ResponsesInList.Text: Steve - I share your pain. I am the architectural lead of a group with about $25 million dollars to spend implementing an Instructional Improvement System for public education. I am not alone. There are currently tens if not hundreds of millions of dollars of grant funding targeted to provisioning Learning Management and Instructional Improvement Systems. It is quite possible that Moodle could play an important role in those efforts, but absent a reasonably well defined architecture that evaluation teams can compare to products that will be: 1) Heavily marketed, 2) Politically connected, and 3) Well defined, it is doubtful that Moodle will be very competetive. ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Moodle documentation: Where is the software architecture documentation?
ResponsesInList.Text: I am struggling with scepticism here. Does being able to draw pretty box diagrams of 'how Moodle's software architecture works' really affect your ability to win contracts like this? Are we trying to understand how Moodle works, or do we just need to win a game of buzz-word bingo? Putting cynicism aside, I will try to address the issues you raise. Your question also suffers from the same issue as using a CV (resume) to apply for jobs. It is well known that you can't just have a CV that you you use to apply for all jobs. You need to taylor your CV to the job and the company you are applying for. Getting back to to Moodle's architecture. The point is not diagrams. The point is that the people evaluating your proposal want to know that moodle has certain non-functional requirements (scalability, maintainability, extensibility, robustness, database-independance, ...) They want sufficient evidence to justify whatever you are claiming, and your judgement is that they will consider an appropriate architecture diagram as sufficient evidence. It is worth noting that there is an assumption there. Before you go looking for a diagram, make sure there are not more compelling forms of evidence. For example, to demonstrate scalability, you may be better using the data on http://moodle.org/stats/ . There may be more information about Moodle in the pubic domain because it is open sourece. Going back to the CV analogy, almost any CV I write for myself is likely to mention that I have several degress. These standard qualifications compactly summarise a lot of evidence about ability - at least in the context of job recruitments. There are, of course, discussions to be had about whether degrees are really the best training for any given job, and whether that is the purpose of education in the first place, but it is still the case that for many jobs, having a degree is a big help when applying. Similarly, there are common architectural patterns that are widely recognised, and if we can draw a standard diagram to show that Moodle works that way, then it would be helpful. But there is still the tayloring issue. I and others here know quite well and are happy to try to explain it, but we don't at-all know your target audience. To get the diagrams you want, perhpas the most effective route is for you to ask us questions about how Moodle works, then once you understand enough, you can express the information is the way that your target audience requires. It has already been mentioned in this thread, but you may find some of the diagrams in http://www.slideshare.net/tjh1000/a-basic-introduciton-to-the-moodle-architecture-5442122 helpful as a starting point. P.S. I have just spotted a beautiful example of just the point I am trying to make. Reading back through the post before hitting send, I realised that talking about CVs (curriculum vitaes) might not mean much to you. In the USA they are more normally called resumes, so I had to add the bracket in the second paragraph. Of course, this sort of thing comes as no suprise to someone who knows about Moodle's pedagogic origins (point 4 of http://docs.moodle.org/20/en/Pedagogy#Social_Constructionism_as_a_Referent ). There is also that standard bit that you get on HR courses, the Shannon and Weaver model of communication ( http://stevefournier01.tripod.com/hist/hist-6.html ). To successfully transmit a message, you can't just thing about how the message you want to send, and how you are going to transmit it. The receiver must correctly interpret your message for any communication to take place.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Moodle documentation: Where is the software architecture documentation?
ResponsesInList.Text: When people in the UK talk about "the difference between political with a capital P and a simple p?" this is what they mean: With a capital P, Politics is specifically about the running the country, political parties, memebers of parliamen, and the media circus that is Westminster. With a small p, politics is just about what happens when people come together and have meetings and have to decide things. As Moodlers, we should really not be surprised at this.
